children.text: St. Jerome Church in Morong was built in stone around 1620 and gained its ornate Baroque facade and octagonal bell tower in 1850–53, making it one of Rizal's landmark old churches. It was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2025 and makes an easy day trip from Manila.

Morong is a small town in Rizal, about 45 km east of Manila on the northeastern shore of Laguna de Bay. The Spanish found a riverside settlement here in 1572 and called it "Moron," and from 1578 the Franciscan missionaries Juan de Plasencia and Diego de Oropesa are said to have begun their mission in the area. The Church of St. Jerome (San Geronimo), standing on a hill in the middle of town, shows more than 400 years of that history.

The first church was a modest building of bamboo, nipa and timber that burned along with the town in a fire in 1612. The Franciscans then built a new church of stone and mortar on higher ground across the river, and a widely cited account says construction began in 1615 and was completed in 1620. Tradition holds that Chinese craftsmen built it, and the Chinese lion statues that flanked the entrance driveway are often cited as a trace of that. Sources differ slightly on the years, so the exact dates are hard to state with certainty.

The ornate facade you see today dates from the 1850s. Fr. Maximo Rico commissioned Bartolome Palatino, a craftsman from Paete, to renovate the facade and build a new bell tower, and the work took place between 1850 and 1853. The three-storey facade and octagonal bell tower are counted among the most beautiful and tallest of any Franciscan church in the Philippines. Morong Church was recognized as a National Cultural Treasure in 2025, in the same year as the churches of Baras and Tanay in Rizal.

For travelers, Morong Church is a quiet heritage stop that is not crowded. The church alone takes just over an hour, but if you walk on to the old arched bridge and the Comandancia museum nearby, you get a real feel for a small Spanish colonial town. It fits well into a day trip along Manila East Road linking the Laguna de Bay lakeside towns.

The facade, with columns stacked in three tiers, is made up of Doric columns, a semicircular arched entrance and a decorated pediment. A statue of St. Jerome stands in the center of the third tier, and the Franciscan coat of arms is said to be carved above it. The facade is also recognized as a tourist spot by the Department of Tourism.

blocks.title: Octagonal Bell Tower and Lighthouse-Like Cross

children.text: The octagonal bell tower rising above the facade has angel statues at its four corners symbolizing the cardinal virtues, and it is topped by a statue of the Archangel St. Michael. The cross at the tip is lit at night and is said to have served as a guide for fishermen on the lake.

blocks.title: A Nave of Stone and Lime

children.text: The nave is a single hall with a semicircular apse. The townspeople are said to have built it from stone from Kay Ngaya hill, lime from Kay Maputi mountain, sand and gravel from the Morong River, and donated timber. The municipal introduction also records that women and children were put to work on it.

The church is said to hold a first-class relic donated to the parish after a pilgrimage in 2005 and a larger relic received in 2007. The larger one is set into the main altar table, while the smaller one is displayed to the faithful at the Saturday anticipated Mass and is kissed on the last Saturday of each month.

Chinese lion sculptures are said to have stood on both sides of the steep entrance driveway. One was stolen between 2000 and 2005, and the other is reportedly kept near the St. Jerome school. They support the tradition that Chinese craftsmen took part in building the church.

During the Philippine Revolution, Spanish soldiers and civil guards were besieged in the church and convent and surrendered to the Katipuneros on August 19, 1898. In 1939 the Philippine Historical Committee is said to have installed a commemorative plaque.

After World War II, the Columban priest Fr. Hugh O'Reilly led the restoration of the dome, which was blessed on January 30, 1949. Further repairs followed, including work on the facade and belfry in the 1960s, and some sources say the dome carries paintings of the evangelists by Botong Francisco.

blocks.title: Puente de San Geronimo and the Old Town Center

children.text: Close to the church are an old arch bridge known to have been built in 1696–1701 (the original is said to have been blown up in World War II), a guardhouse, a signal bell tower, and the Comandancia, the Spanish-era seat of government. The second floor of the Comandancia is said to serve as a municipal museum. Together with the church, it makes a pleasant small-town walking route.

items.title: Half-Day Route
items.subtitle: The church and the old town center

children.text: Leave Manila and head to Morong via Manila East Road (R-6) or the roads from Antipolo. Depending on traffic it can take
2 hours to 2 hours 30 minutes
or more, so allow extra time.

From the bottom of the entrance driveway, look up at the full facade and bell tower first, then climb the steps to the churchyard and look at the facade decoration and the place where the Chinese lion statues stood.
When no Mass is being held, step quietly into the nave and look at the altar, choir loft and dome ceiling. Knowing that a relic of St. Jerome lies at the main altar adds meaning to the visit.
Head down into town for lunch, then walk around the Comandancia museum, the guardhouse and the old arched bridge. Check the museum's opening hours locally.
Stop at one more lakeside town or nearby church, or return to Manila.
Interior photography and opening hours vary with Masses and events, so it is safest to check the parish's announcements before you arrive.

items.title: Laguna de Bay Church Circuit
items.subtitle: A one-day route in eastern Rizal

children.text: Leave Manila and head east along the lakeside road through Taytay, Angono and Binangonan.
See St. Jerome Church in Morong and check the facade and bell tower to understand why it was declared a National Cultural Treasure.
After lunch, continue toward Pililla or Tanay and visit other National Cultural Treasure churches such as San Ildefonso Church in Tanay.
Set out toward Manila before dark. On weekend evenings the Antipolo side can be congested.

items.title: From Manila by Car or Taxi

children.text: Morong is about
45km
from Manila. The basic route is Manila East Road, which runs along the edge of the lake through Taytay, Angono, Binangonan and Cardona.
From Antipolo it is about
27km
via Sumulong Highway, described as roughly an hour. This varies greatly with traffic.
Entering "Morong Church" or "St. Jerome Parish" into your navigation app will guide you to the hill in the town center.
Travel time varies greatly with departure time and traffic, so check a map app before you leave.

The usual way is to take a jeepney or van bound for eastern Rizal from an eastern terminal (Cubao, Ortigas and so on) and transfer. Exact routes, fares and first and last trip times change, so check locally.
Many travelers also transfer in Antipolo or Taytay onto a Morong- or Tanay-bound ride.
The center of Morong is small enough to explore on foot. The church, the Comandancia and the old arched bridge are not far from one another.
For farther places, take a tricycle; fares depend on distance. Agree on the price before you ride for peace of mind.

Because the purpose is architecture, the cooler, drier months from November to May are best for walking. December to February in particular are relatively mild even at midday, which makes the hill steps easier.

The feast day of the patron saint, St. Jerome, is September 30, so events may be held in town around then. Be prepared for sudden showers and typhoons, though, since June to November is the rainy season.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Morong is usually a day trip, so it is more convenient to stay in Manila or Antipolo. There are small lodgings in town but few choices, so book ahead if you plan to stay the night.

Morong is known for balaw-balaw, a local side dish presented by the municipality. You can eat Filipino home cooking at small restaurants and shops in town, and toward Laguna de Bay there are also places serving lake fish dishes. Check menus and opening hours locally.
A church is a place of worship. Clothing that covers the shoulders and knees is recommended.
During Mass, do not walk along the side aisles or speak loudly, and take photos in a way that does not disturb the priest or worshippers.
The best place to see the whole facade and bell tower is the driveway at the bottom of the steps. The morning light direction is generally good.
A relic display and kissing of the relic are said to take place at the Saturday anticipated Mass and on the last Saturday of each month. Check the schedule with the parish if you want to attend.
The Comandancia, the old arched bridge and the guardhouse are connected on foot, so wear comfortable shoes.
Combine it on the same day with the churches of Baras and Tanay in eastern Rizal for a National Cultural Treasure church circuit.
Bring plenty of cash. Many places outside the town center do not accept cards.
Sources differ on dates and dimensions. For the year of construction and the facade completion date, follow local signage and parish announcements.
On weekends and feast days roads can be congested, so a round trip from Manila may take longer than expected.
Church opening hours and Mass schedules can change, so check the latest announcements.
The steps and driveway in front of the church are steep, so take care when traveling with older people or children.
Guard against pickpockets and touts by keeping your belongings in front of you and never leaving a bag down while taking photos.
In the rainy season the paths can be slippery, so take care on the steps.

blocks.title: Tanay Old Town and San Ildefonso Church

children.text: This is the Tanay church that was declared a National Cultural Treasure in the same year. Continuing from Morong along the lake road, it pairs well in a single day.
A wind farm reached by continuing east of the lake along Manila East Road, which can be combined with a church visit.
An art town on the way from Manila to Morong, good for a stop on the road in or out.
A pilgrimage city about
27km
from Morong, which you can add on the way back.
